Mow- ever, only chemical leaching could separate all three phases of magnetization (a detrital (IIRM) and two chemical (CRM, and CKMB) remanent magnetizations) in Carboniferous red beds (Roy atad Park 1974). Chemical, thermal, and AF cleaning techniques were performed on the Wig Wam red beds. Unfor- tunately, the different phases of magnetization co~~ld not be separated by chemical leaching. The effectiveness of the chemical method is highly de- pendent upon the penetration rate of the acid which is regulated by the porosity and permeability of the rack. Ideally, the rate should be rapid so that the grains carrying the late phase magnetization (red pigmentation CUMB) can be destroyed throughout the specimen before the more resistant (to acid) grains carrying the early phases (DRM and GKMA) are attacked. The Botwood samples are fine- grained sediments and acid penetration is very slow. The slicing of specimens after 2300 h in HCI shows that 15% of the red cement remains in the sample which may mean that in the outer zone all phases are attacked to varying degrees, while in the inner zone none of the phases are destroyed. The effectiveness of the chemical method is highly de- pendent upon the penetration rate of the acid which is regulated by the porosity and permeability of the rack. It should be stated that the lower Paleozoic results have not, in general, been sup- ported by corroborative radiometric results; the age control is then open to discussion. Basically, from Cambrian to Silurian there is a linear trend. From Lower Silurian (3C) to Devonian (4A) there is no data available, except for the Mount Peyton late phase intrusion (3D). This pole is much to the south of 3C and 48. If this I-eally represents the pole location at about 380Ma, then a rapid apparent polar wander occurred during the Devo- nian relative to Newfoundland. This last pole (3D) might also be the first paleomagnetic evidence of an ice age as claimed by McCann and Kennedy (1974) for Newfoundland (paleolatitude = 76"), although the timing of the event seems offset. SYMONS Department of Geology, University of Windsor, Windsor, Ont., Canada N9B 3P4 Received February 23, 1979 Revision accepted May 11, 1979 Oka and nearby small plutons on the western end of the Monteregian Hills were sampled for paleomagnetic study at 43 sites (569 specimens). Every specimen was AF step demagnetized in 4 kA/m increments to 20 or 24 kA/m. Consistent remanence directions were found for 36 sites (452 specimens). Use of a stability index to select only those specimens with the best defined end points does not improve the site statistics. The Oka, Brilund, Carillon, and Ile Cadieux plutons have statistically similar mean remanence direction populations which are different from the Ste. Dorothee sill direction. Except for one Carillon site, all site mean directions are normally polarized, whereas all nine plutons, except for Mt. Johnson, from the middle and eastern end of the Monteregian Hills are reversely polarized. Normally and reversely polarized plutons give statistically similar but antiparallel pole positions, giving a combined pole position of 169.0°W, 72.4"N (6, = 2.8", 8, = 3.7"), which is consistent with the 120 f 4 Ma radiometric age. sedimentary rocks (Williams 1964). In the study area, red and green tuffs and cherts are predomi- nant. The Exploits Group which includes the Point Leamington Formation, consists of greywacke and argillite (Williams 1962). The Leading Tickles dunite is about 1 km long and about 0.5 km wide, and is well exposed along the road to Leading Tickles settlement. It can be best described as a differentiated diabase stock with an olivine rich zone. This intrusion was named by Helwig (1967) and was interpreted as Jurassic in age based on correlation with the Budgell Harbour Gabbro and related lamprophyres. However, using geochemical and petrographical work as a correla- tive factor, Harris (1973) suggested an Ordovician age for the Leading Tickles dunite. The lamprophyres dikes were first described by Hey1 (1935) as monchiquites and fourchites, al- though Helwig (1967) indicated that the most com- mon are vogesite, spessartite, and kersantite. They range from minor veinlets to dikes 1 m in thickness, most of them being vertical to subvertical, and dominantly northeast trending. The Jurassic-Cretaceous (1 10- 150 Ma) and the Cretaceous-Tertiary (50-81 Ma) boundary are characterized by atnixed polarity interval. It is then probable that the lamprophyre dikes were intruded during the Cretaceous normal (81- 110 Ma) polarity interval. It should be noted that an alternative ex- planation would be that the dikes were intruded in a normal polarity time within a mixed polarity inter- val. This explanation implies that the time of intru- sion and the cooling rate of these dikes were rapid and it would also imply that no chemically acquired remanences are present. Since this explanation is more demanding, the previous explanation is favoured. So, if the dikes were intruded in the nor- mal polarity interval, then the Mont Megantic (172"E, 69"N) and the Monteregian Hills paleopoles (203"E, 65"N and 190°E, 71°N, Larochelle 1968) are probably slightly older than the Notre Dame Bay lamprophyre dikes. Their results show mixed polarities, associating the intrusions with the Juras- sic-Cretaceous mixed polarity interval. The Leading Tickles dunite is about 1 km long and about 0.5 km wide, and is well exposed along the road to Leading Tickles settlement. It can be best described as a differentiated diabase stock with an olivine rich zone. This intrusion was named by Helwig (1967) and was interpreted as Jurassic in age based on correlation with the Budgell Harbour Gabbro and related lamprophyres. The Jurassic-Cretaceous (1 10- 150 Ma) and the Cretaceous-Tertiary (50-81 Ma) boundary are characterized by atnixed polarity interval. It is then probable that the lamprophyre dikes were intruded during the Cretaceous normal (81- 110 Ma) polarity interval. It should be noted that an alternative ex- planation would be that the dikes were intruded in a normal polarity time within a mixed polarity inter- val. This explanation implies that the time of intru- sion and the cooling rate of these dikes were rapid and it would also imply that no chemically acquired remanences are present. Since this explanation is more demanding, the previous explanation is favoured. So, if the dikes were intruded in the nor- mal polarity interval, then the Mont Megantic (172"E, 69"N) and the Monteregian Hills paleopoles (203"E, 65"N and 190°E, 71°N, Larochelle 1968) are probably slightly older than the Notre Dame Bay lamprophyre dikes. From 16 sites, 197 specimens were subjected to stepwise thermal treatments to 710°C, and a further 46 to incremental af cleaning to 290 mT. The 10 sites from the unshocked St-Urbain anorthosite carry a magnetization with unblocking temperatures (TUB) generally between 600-625°C. with a significant fraction of remanence with TUB > 670°C. Similarly, most of the remanence has a resistive coercive force (rcf) of 100-175 mT, with a significant fraction exceed- ing 290 mT. The remanence is carried by two exsolution phases of titano-hematite, with the later and more hematite-rich lamellae having the higher TUB and rcf. Although only one direction exists, at two sites where intensities are somewhat lower and some natural remanent magnetiza- tion (NRM) directions scattered, treatment reveals a dual polarity remanence. The pole (154"E, 02"s) obtained from these unshocked St-Urbain anorthosite sites falls on a well estab- lished segment of the late Precambrian apparent polar path of suitable age (~950 Ma). Significant results could not be o6tained from three additional sites in the marginal zone due to their ready acquisition of a viscous magnetization following thermal treat

uld not be o6tained from three additional sites in the marginal zone due to their ready acquisition of a viscous magnetization following thermal treatments. Data from two sites which display no shock effects and lie near the margin of the central uplift, and from one highly shocked sample from the crater centre show some possible effects of the shock event. All three have intensities substantially lower than in the St-Urbain sites, which is interpreted in the case of at least one of these sites as a shock-diminished remanence. A puzzling feature of the highly shocked samples is that the phase with a texture reminiscent of the ilmenite-hematite exsolution in the unshocked anorthosites, contains no iron. The remaining remanence, whose direction is parallel with that of the unshocked sites, is interpreted as pre- crater rather than shock-produced. Although many instances have been reported of a new shock-induced remanence imparted to rocks of equivalent and even lesser shock grade than those examined at Charlevoix, in all cases the magnetic carrier seems to have been magnetite. The lack of a shock-induced (emanence at Charlevoix is attributed to the high TUB and rcf of hematite in these rocks. A few formations show only group 1 or only group 2 NRM's, but most have examples of both, frequently superimposed in individual samples. Superimposed (or multicomponent) NRM's were separable in two cases: (I) if one component was completely demagnetized at high AF steps, so that the remanence vector reached a stable endpoint direction or (2) if one component was not demag- netized at all over some AF range, usually at low AF steps, so that the direction of the other compo- nent could be deduced by the Zijderveld diagram vector-subtraction technique (Zijderveld 1967). Otherwise, although the magnetization vector fol- lowed a "remagnetization circle" (Halls 1976) joining groups 1 and 2, neither component could be isolated from the data and used in defining the mean group directions. Group 1 directions tend to have north (or south) declinations and intermediate (40-65") inclinations. Group 2 directions tend to have shal- low inclinations with east to northeast (or west to southwest) declinations. Reversals of the paleofield are recorded in both groups. The proportion of normal and reversed samples is variable and not close to 50:50, suggesting infrequent reversals. A few formations show only group 1 or only group 2 NRM's, but most have examples of both, frequently superimposed in individual samples. Superimposed (or multicomponent) NRM's were separable in two cases: (I) if one component was completely demagnetized at high AF steps, so that the remanence vector reached a stable endpoint direction or (2) if one component was not demag- netized at all over some AF range, usually at low AF steps, so that the direction of the other compo- nent could be deduced by the Zijderveld diagram vector-subtraction technique (Zijderveld 1967). Otherwise, although the magnetization vector fol- lowed a "remagnetization circle" (Halls 1976) joining groups 1 and 2, neither component could be isolated from the data and used in defining the mean group directions. 1965). The trend of these anomalies (and thus the general strike of the dikes) is parallel to the Lake Superior rift axis (Halls 1978). Although there are no radiometric age data for the dikes, Aldrich et al. (1965) report a whole-rock K-Ar age of 960 Ma for an unmetamorphosed diabase dike in Iron County south of Baraga County. If this dike is coeval with the main swarm, then the Baraga-Marquette dikes are Keweenawan in age. The relative age of the dike swarm can be defined within broad limits based on geological field relations. They intrude both the Archean and Animikean rocks and show distinct chilled margins (Graham 1953; Gair and Thaden 1968; Cannon and Klasner 1972). Petrologically the dikes have not been affected by the last post-Animikean meta- morphism at about 1.7Ga ago (Van Schmus and Woolsley 1975). This relation is clearly shown by the aeromagnetic data as an increase in wavelength of dike anomalies on the western side of the contact between the Jacobsville and older rocks (Meshref and Hinze 1970). Although there are no radiometric age data for the dikes, Aldrich et al. (1965) report a whole-rock K-Ar age of 960 Ma for an unmetamorphosed diabase dike in Iron County south of Baraga County. Magnetic Mineralogy Eight thin sections of sites from two sites each of the northwest-up, north-up, and north-northeast- down groups of magnetic directions were examined with a microscope. The rocks are plagiophyric basalts which sometimes contain augite pheno- crysts. Large amygdules and interstitial openings are filled with chlorite, quartz, epidote, and pre- hnite, and suggest shallow water or subaerial extru- sion. Metamorphism corresponds to pumpel- lyite-prehnite or low-greenschist facies. Pyroxene is generally replaced by amphibole. Magnetite is fairly abundant and is variably altered to sphene but in most cases alteration is minor. Magnetic Mineralogy Eight thin sections of sites from two sites each of the northwest-up, north-up, and north-northeast- down groups of magnetic directions were examined with a microscope. The rocks are plagiophyric basalts which sometimes contain augite pheno- crysts. Large amygdules and interstitial openings are filled with chlorite, quartz, epidote, and pre- hnite, and suggest shallow water or subaerial extru- sion. Metamorphism corresponds to pumpel- lyite-prehnite or low-greenschist facies. Pyroxene is generally replaced by amphibole. Magnetite is fairly abundant and is variably altered to sphene but in most cases alteration is minor. In detail, the samples showing the north- northeast-down magnetization (e.g., site 69) dis- play relatively strong alteration with all pyroxene replaced by amphibole. In contrast to this, all sam- ples from sites 50 and 51 show only weak alteration of pyroxenes (northwest-up direction) with some oxydization of magnetite to possibly haematite. The samples from site 58 and 59 showing the north-up direction show very similar features to those from the northwest-up sites. The magnetic mineralogy was also studied with a recording thermomagnet

There are, of course, an infinite number of ways to get these poles to coincide by different combinations of northward shift and rota- tion which would result in other source areas for the Karmutsen volcanics but these must all include a large northerly directed component of motion. The age of the northwest-up direction occurring in 20% of the sites has not been established, not even with respect to the folding. Magnetic Mineralogy Eight thin sections of sites from two sites each of the northwest-up, north-up, and north-northeast- down groups of magnetic directions were examined with a microscope. The rocks are plagiophyric basalts which sometimes contain augite pheno- crysts. Large amygdules and interstitial openings are filled with chlorite, quartz, epidote, and pre- hnite, and suggest shallow water or subaerial extru- sion. Metamorphism corresponds to pumpel- lyite-prehnite or low-greenschist facies. Pyroxene is generally replaced by amphibole. Magnetite is fairly abundant and is variably altered to sphene but in most cases alteration is minor. In detail, the samples showing the north- northeast-down magnetization (e.g., site 69) dis- play relatively strong alteration with all pyroxene replaced by amphibole. In contrast to this, all sam- ples from sites 50 and 51 show only weak alteration of pyroxenes (northwest-up direction) with some oxydization of magnetite to possibly haematite. The samples from site 58 and 59 showing the north-up direction show very similar features to those from the northwest-up sites. The magnetic mineralogy was also studied with a recording thermomagnet

There are, of course, an infinite number of ways to get these poles to coincide by different combinations of northward shift and rota- tion which would result in other source areas for the Karmutsen volcanics but these must all include a large northerly directed component of motion. The age of the northwest-up direction occurring in 20% of the sites has not been established, not even with respect to the folding. Only circumstan- tial evidence (high oxydation state, relatively sim- ple magnetic mineralogy, high coercivity single component) suggests that it might be authentic. However, even if it is secondary, comparison with the post-Triassic part of the apparent polar wander curve for cratonic North America shows an even larger anomaly which then might suggest an even larger northward movement of the area in a shorter time span. Smith and Busby [1993] reported a \"slump\" test and a fold test for the middle Cretaceous Pinos Formation on Cedros Island. As pointed out by Butler and Dickinson [1995], the slump test is inconclusive because there is no statistical improvement (inclination only) after structural correction of the mean direc- tions for all blocks. In response, Smith and Busby [1995] claimed a positive conglomerate test because the in situ data for the slump blocks have random directions. This is only half the test, however, and unslumped Pinos Formation must also be shown to carry a nonrandom characteristic magnetization. The fold test for the Pinos Formation on Cedros Island includes data from the Valle Formation on the Vizcaino Peninsula [Patterson, 1984], but the age of deformation and, thus, of magnetization acquisition in the two areas is uncertain. 4.2. The X magnetizations are consistent in direc- tion through a great stratigraphic thickness and are characterized by high unblocking temperatures and fields (coercivities). The unblocking temperatures and fields are a measure of the "hardness" of the remanent magnetization (Zijderveld 1975). We also showed that other magnetizations (here called Y but referred to previously as A) with less consistent directions and lower unblocking temperatures and fields were present. We argued that Y was a secon- dary overprint, probably acquired during the Juras- sic, because it was less hard and because the direc- tions were roughly along the expected Jurassic field. Samples were collected from the Akaitcho River Formation which represents a small fraction of the Great Slave Supergroup - a sequence of some 8000 m of sedimentary rocks deposited be- tween about 2200 and 1800 Ma ago. Earth Sci., 17, 1583-1588 (1980) [Traduit par le journal] Introduction The occurrence of minor igneous intrusions in the Valley and Ridge province of Virginia and West Virginia has long been known (Darton and Diller 1890; Darton and Keith 1898). The intrusions are mostly northwest-striking dikes, cutting tightly folded limestone, shales, and sandstones of Or- dovician to Devonian age (Fig. 1). Although the intrusions of Pendleton County, West Virginia are predominately basalts, a wide variety of igneous rock types are represented; in Highland County, Virginia, andesites are more numerous. On the basis of petrographic resemblances to other eastern North American dikes, Garner (1956) assumed the basalts to be of Triassic age. The andesites had been postulated to be related to the Devonian Tioga bentonite. It came as a surprise, therefore, when Fullagar and Bottino (1969) determined an Eocene age for biotites from the andesite. Several geophysical anomalies are located near the Eocene rocks and may be causally related to them (Dennison and Johnson 1971; Bollinger and Gilbert 1974). These include the most extensive concentration of thermal springs in eastern North America, an 'earthquake shadow zone' with re- duced surface disturbances associa

on and Johnson 1971) have noted that the intrusions are situated along a long lasting, deep seated zone of crustal weakness. The recognition of olivine basalts as contem- poraneous with the more felsic rocks makes Denni- son and Johnson's (1971) argument for derivation from a granitic pluton appear dubious, while Hall's (1974) proposal for fractional crystallization of a basaltic magma is strengthened. The Eocene magnetic directions obtained from units of volcanic breccia and diatreme suggest a shallow depth of dike emplacement and possible volcanism. 1588 CAN. J. EARTH SCI. Subsequent K-Ar dating, however, has shown this dike to be about 46Ma old and this direction has therefore been included in our mean result. The dike is slightly altered to the extent that olivine has been replaced by antigorite (Garner 1956), and secondary magne- tite may have formed during the serpentinization process. Alternately, the dike may have acquired its magnetization during an excursion. broic plutons during Middle Devonian time (Gates 1969). Numerous faults cut and disrupt the coastal volcanic belt, the major ones striking northeast to east and generally having steep dips. Deformation probably began in the Silurian and continued intermittently to post-Triassic time, al- though many of the major faults were active mostly in Carboniferous and (or) Triassic times (Webb 1969). The coastal volcanic sequence reaches a maxi- mum thickness of about 14000 m in the Eastport quadrangle of southeastern Maine where we have concentrated our paleomagnetic studies. Mapping of this area was originally done by Bastin and Wil- liams (1914) and more recently by Gates (1975), from whose work the geological sketch map in Fig. 1 is drawn. The bulk of the rocks consists of a heterogeneous suite of fossiliferous marine sedimentary and volcanic rocks. They lie in a gen- erally conformable sequence with some interton- guing, and are overlain with angular unconformity by the Upper Devonian Perry Formation. The Perry Formation, however, is also tilted, in some localities to near-vertical but typically about 20", and also cut by faults. Partial demagnetization experiments and vector differences indicate that the magnetization involved is multicomponent, with a well-defined overprint masking an underlying magnetic component. The overprint has now been recognized in many formations of the Great Slave Supergroup and is interpreted as having been acquired in response to uplift and cooling following orogeny in the Coronation Geosyncline. A population of intermediate blocking temperature components, K2, is post-tectonic and found only in the Fond du Lac Formation and Middle River section. Poles calculated from K2 fall among the Grenville type poles (Fond du Lac, 9"S, 145"E; Middle River, 24"S, 162OE). A third population of components, K3, has low blocking temperature and coercivity and is isolated only by chemical leaching. K3 has steep positive inclination, northern declination, and is post-tectonic. It is interpreted as a recent magnetization. Any interpretation of the path of apparent polar wander for North America must accommodate the sequence of magnetization K1 to K2. The timing of tectonism in the Keweenawan basin is bracketed by the times of acquisition of K1 and K2. These results reconfirm some recent interpretations that include Grenville poles on the polar wander trackof interior Laurentia. The Fond du Lac Formation consists of subarkosic and arko- sic shales, siltstones, and sandstones with a basal con- glomerate, probably representing a wedge of clastic material deposited in an oxidizing deltaic environment. These rocks crop out in a limited area along the St. Louis River and a small tributary, Mission Creek, near Duluth, Minnesota (Fig. 1). Linearity of a demagnetization trajectory on an orthogonal projection may be regarded as a determination of the spectral window of demagne- tization over which a component is isolated (Dunlop 1979). Components, so determined, were isolated by vector subtraction of the two results that best defined the linear trajectory. For example, refemng to Fig. 2b, one component is isolated by vector subtraction of the re- manences measured after treatments of 550 and 640°C, and a second component is isolated by subtraction of the remanences measured after treatments of 650 and 670°C. Components were classified on the basis of coercivity, blocking temperature, and resistance to leaching. With the exception of a single site in the Fond du Lac Formation, there was good correlation between the directions and the physical properties of the compo- nents. Components with high blocking temperatures (650-670°C) and coercivities greater than 100 mT and that resist leaching in 8 N HC1 for up to 50-100 h were found in nearly all samples. The stratigraphy and petrology of the Fond du Lac Formation have been summarized by Morey (1967) and much of the following description is from that work. The Fond du Lac Formation consists of subarkosic and arko- sic shales, siltstones, and sandstones with a basal con- glomerate, probably representing a wedge of clastic material deposited in an oxidizing deltaic environment. These rocks crop out in a limited area along the St. Louis River and a small tributary, Mission Creek, near Duluth, Minnesota (Fig. 1). The Fond du Lac exceeds 244 m in thickness, but only 90 m is now exposed. The red color is due to hematite, which occurs as a coating on the surfaces of sand- and silt-sized quartz and feldspar grains or occupying the interstices between the grains. Hematite was probably formed in place, sometime after deposition and prior to complete lithification. A further source of hematite may be the alteration of detrital iron-bearing silicate minerals such as pyroxene, horn- blende, and biotite. Linearity of a demagnetization trajectory on an orthogonal projection may be regarded as a determination of the spectral window of demagne- tization over which a component is isolated (Dunlop 1979). Components, so determined, were isolated by vector subtraction of the two results that best defined the linear trajectory. For example, refemng to Fig. 2b, one component is isolated by vector subtraction of the re- manences measured after treatments of 550 and 640°C, and a second component is isolated by subtraction of the remanences measured after treatments of 650 and 670°C. Components were classified on the basis of coercivity, blocking temperature, and resistance to leaching. With the exception of a single site in the Fond du Lac Formation, there was good correlation between the directions and the physical properties of the compo- nents. Components with high blocking temperatures (650-670°C) and coercivities greater than 100 mT and that resist leaching in 8 N HC1 for up to 50-100 h were found in nearly all samples. Components with these properties were assigned to the K1 population. A second set of components, assigned to the K2 population, had blocking temperatures between 400 and 640°C, coerci- vities greater than 100 mT, and were the first compo- nents to be removed by leaching. The stratigraphy and petrology of the Fond du Lac Formation have been summarized by Morey (1967) and much of the following description is from that work. The Fond du Lac Formation consists of subarkosic and arko- sic shales, siltstones, and sandstones with a basal con- glomerate, probably representing a wedge of clastic material deposited in an oxidizing deltaic environment. These rocks crop out in a limited area along the St. Louis River and a small tributary, Mission Creek, near Duluth, Minnesota (Fig. 1). The Fond du Lac exceeds 244 m in thickness, but only 90 m is now exposed. The red color is due to hematite, which occurs as a coating on the surfaces of sand- and silt-sized quartz and feldspar grains or occupying the interstices between the grains. Hematite was probably formed in place, sometime after deposition and prior to complete lithification. A further source of hematite may be the alteration of detrital iron-bearing silicate minerals such as pyroxene, horn- blende, and biotite. The correlation and absolute age of the Fond du Lac Formation have long been problems. Linearity of a demagnetization trajectory on an orthogonal projection may be regarded as a determination of the spectral window of demagne- tization over which a component is isolated (Dunlop 1979). Components, so determined, were isolated by vector subtraction of the two results that best defined the linear trajectory. For example, refemng to Fig. 2b, one component is isolated by vector subtraction of the re- manences measured after treatments of 550 and 640°C, and a second component is isolated by subtraction of the remanences measured after treatments of 650 and 670°C. Components were classified on the basis of coercivity, blocking temperature, and resistance to leaching. With the exception of a single site in the Fond du Lac Formation, there was good correlation between the directions and the physical properties of the compo- nents. Components with high blocking temperatures (650-670°C) and coercivities greater than 100 mT and that resist leaching in 8 N HC1 for up to 50-100 h were found in nearly all samples. Components with these properties were assigned to the K1 population. A second set of components, assigned to the K2 population, had blocking temperatures between 400 and 640°C, coerci- vities greater than 100 mT, and were the first compo- nents to be removed by leaching. ng field (AF) and thermal experiments performed on the younger granites indicate that they are characterized by three different mean directions of magnetization in the 10-60 mT coercivity spectra: SE (D = 149", 1 = $70"; K = 160, N = 4 sites); NE-1 (D = 72", 1 = -70"; K = 320, N = 3 sites); andNE-2 (D = 31°, 1 = -24"; K = 67, N = 3 sites) with corresponding paleopole positions at CB-1 (16'N, 41%'; Sp, Sm = 6", 7"); CB-2 (32"N, 97"W; Sp, Sm = 7", 8"); and CB-3 (27"S, 96%'; Sp, Sm = 6", 1 lo). The radiometric ages of these three remanence directions do not differ from each other by more than 50 Ma; these remanences are also present as low coercivity (5-25 mT) magnetizations in the Avalonian granites (10 sites). Antipole CB-3 agrees with other recently reported Early Devonian paleomagnetic results from the northern Appalachians. In contrast, the two other antipoles (CB-1 and CB-2) are located in southerly latitudes but do not differ significantly from poles of contemporaneous rocks in New Brunswick and Newfoundland. The "aberrancy" of southerly located Siluro-Devonian poles with respect to those in northern latitudes is discussed in the context of possible transcurrent motion of the "Acadia" displaced terrain with respect to cratonic North America. Presently available paleomagnet

ontemporaneous rocks in New Brunswick and Newfoundland. The "aberrancy" of southerly located Siluro-Devonian poles with respect to those in northern latitudes is discussed in the context of possible transcurrent motion of the "Acadia" displaced terrain with respect to cratonic North America. Presently available paleomagnetic data are not conclusive and cannot confirm or negate this possibility. The CB-1, CB-2, and CB-3 poles are interpreted as representing rapid apparent polar wander with respect to Cape Breton Island during Siluro-Devonian time. In the older Cambrian granites, pole CB (37"N, 176"E; Sp, Sm = 2", 3'), derived from a high coercivity (20-70 mT) mean remanence direction NW (D = 318", 1 = +ISo; K = 298, N = 10 sites), probably corresponds to the Avalonian Orogeny. Further results are needed to interpret the paleogeographic setting of the Avalon microcontinent in early Paleozoic time. The "aberrancy" of southerly located Siluro-Devonian poles with respect to those in northern latitudes is discussed in the context of possible transcurrent motion of the "Acadia" displaced terrain with respect to cratonic North America. Presently available paleomagnetic data are not conclusive and cannot confirm or negate this possibility. The "aberrancy" of southerly located Siluro-Devonian poles with respect to those in northern latitudes is discussed in the context of possible transcurrent motion of the "Acadia" displaced terrain with respect to cratonic North America. The Mafic Complex northwest of Boston is a hyp- abyssal association of rapidly varying gabbros, diabase, and basalt dikes, granite and aplite tongues and string- ers, and hydrothermal alterations in no fixed sequence. The rocks are often laced with epidote veinlets giving them a stewed appearance in outcrop. Microscopically the rocks of the Mafic Complex are metagabbro, metadiabase, and somewhat less altered thin basalt dikes, where not veined. The pyroxenes are generally totally replaced by a uralitic hornblende, magnetite, epidote, biotite, or chlorite and the plagioclase is mostly replaced by saussurite, epidote, calcite, and sericite. The plagioclase is commonly in the range An2u5; much of it has been albitized, with CaO going into epidote and calcite. The opaques are commonly distributed in close relationship with the alteration products.The rocks have often been invaded to a varying extent by granitic apophyses down in size to aplite stringers. The perva- sive hydrothermal alteration involved introduction of large total proportions of H20 and O2 and produced a major metasomatism without shearing. Subsequently a detailed thermal and alternating field (AF) demagnetization study of seven Copper Harbor flows by Vincenz and Yaskawa (1968) revealed stable end points having a much lower inclination (D = 282", I = 12'). These authors inferred that the higher inclina- tion obtained by Dubois was because his samples, not having been demagnetized, still retained a small viscous remanent magnetization (VRM) component directed along the present Earth's field. The reduction in NRM intensity of lava flows (Fig. 6) and the higher blocking temperatures of either S1 and S2 component compared to P demonstrate that the overprinting is a CRM. A westward increase in CRM overprinting within the Copper Harbor Formation found initially from the pebble data (Palmer et al. 198 1) has thus been confirmed from study of in situ lava flows. Subsequently a detailed thermal and alternating field (AF) demagnetization study of seven Copper Harbor flows by Vincenz and Yaskawa (1968) revealed stable end points having a much lower inclination (D = 282", I = 12'). These authors inferred that the higher inclina- tion obtained by Dubois was because his samples, not having been demagnetized, still retained a small viscous remanent magnetization (VRM) component directed along the present Earth's field. On first consideration it would seem likely that these poles are virtual geomagnetic poles (vgp) or spot readings of the direction of the Earth's magnetic field, because all of the useful results were obtained from what appears to be a single sill that presumably cooled within a relatively short time compared with the secular variation period of the Earth's field. Calculations made using the method and basic assumptions of Thorning and Abrahamsen (1980) appear to confirm this contention, for they indicate that the 20-60 m thick sill of this study buried at a depth of at least 3.5 km would have cooled through the main AR TUB interval of 400-300°C in a period of 100-200 years as compared with a probable duration of the secular variation cycle of roughly 5000-20000 years. Earth Sci., 18, 1572-1580 (1981) [Traduit par le journal] Introduction The stratigraphic succession within the Mackenzie Mountains Supergroup of the Canadian Cordillera is given in Table 1. An unconformity above the Little Dal Group presumably divides this Precambrian succession into Helikian and Hadrynian age sequences. All of these units to at least as high as the "grainstone subunit" of the Little Dal Group are cut by diabase intrusions, which are thought to be lithologically equivalent to the diabase sills sampled for the present study within the Tsezotene Formation (Aitken and Cook 1974). The porphyritic basaltic Little Dal lavas occurring at the top of the Little Dal Group are probably unrelated to the sills (Aitken 1980; Moms and Park 1981). The sills are found only in the Tsezotene Formation, predominantly in the upper 150 m. In some areas three or more sills are present, but one major sill ranging from about 18 to 60m thick 'Contribution from the Earth Physics Branch No. 945. appears to be of regional extent (Aitken and Cook 1974). Conclusions Paleomagnetic study of dike samples taken from parts of the northeasterly trending Caraquet dike system, associated with the trans-New Brunswick aeromagnetic lineament, resulted in the determination of paleopoles 7a (143%, 78%), 7b (133%, 74%), and 7c (82%, 62%) for the three widely separated sampling areas C (353", +56O), N (353", +50°), and T (14", +37"), respectively. Determination of these virtual pole positions is based on stable remanence directions carried by titanomagnetite. In contrast to pole 7c, which agrees well with other Late Triassic - Early Jurassic poles for the Appalachians, poles 7a and 7b are significantly different and fall in the general area of average paleopoles computed for Mid- dle-Late Jurassic age. A likely possibility that the age of the dike at T differs from that of dikes at C and N by at least 20Ma is suggested but this is tentative since paleomagnetic data are based on a limited number of samples. In the absence of reliable radiometric data, it is premature at the present stage to predict with certainty the likely occurrence of younger magnetization in some of these dikes.

Because reversals of the geomagnetic field were frequent in the Late Triassic, it is not possible to determine the hemisphere or origin, so the net displacement since the Late Triassic could have been something in excess of 1000 km from northern palaeolatitudes or 5000 km from southern palaeolatitudes. Determinations of relative displacement critically depend on the accuracy with which the reference palaeopoles of the craton are known. Recent revisions of the geological time-scale (Harland er al. 1952; Kent & Gradstein 1985) have transferred what used to be the main source of Late Triassic reference information (the Newark Supergroup) from the Late Triassic into the Early Jurassic. Moreover, palaeopoles from older (Early Jurassic) and from younger (Middle Jurassic) Newark rocks are significantly different, showing that the earlier Jurassic was an interval of rapid apparent polar movement (Smith & Noltimier 1979). Small areas of the underlying Mississagi and overlying Lorrain clastic sediments are present. The Gowganda Formation comprises polymictic conglomerate, quartz arenite, arkose, and argillite and has a maximum thickness of 1500m (Roscoe 1973). It gives a concordant early Aphebian Rb-Sr whole-rock isochron age of 2290 + 90 Ma (Fairbairn et al. 1969). The Gowganda Formation has been extensively in- truded by Nipissing sills in the study area. The sills are composed of subophitic gabbro, diabase, and late quartz monzonite differentiates. Some of these irregutar sills are hundreds of metres thick (Dressler 1979). Twenty-one oolitic hematite samples from nine sites were thermally demag- netized in 10 or 11 steps to 660 or 680°C. At 450°C, 15 samples from six sites define a stable magnetization direction (D = 21.2", 1 = -12.S0, k = 137, ag5 = 5.7") with respect to bedding. The remaining six samples failed to attain the stable end-point, five of them because of growth of much "magnetite," which probably resulted from breakdown of siderite during thermal demagnetization. The paleopole for the Wabana - Bell Island Groups lies at 33ON 102"E (dm = 5.8", dp = 3.0"). It is compared with other early Paleozoic paleopoles from cratonic North America and the Avalon zone, and its significance for the Iapetus Ocean is discussed. The oolitic hematites were first studied paleomagnetically by Rao (1970), who reported a well defined remanence direction after thermal demagnetiza- tion to 685°C. The corresponding paleopole at 28"N, 192"E (Deutsch and Rao 1970, 1977tsignificantly to the east of other Ordovician paleopoles for North America-has been used to position the Avalonian microcontinent in early Paleozoic continental recon- structions (e.g., Scotese et al. 1979). The only other early Paleozoic paleopole then available for the Avalon zone was from the red beds of the Ratcliffe Brook Formation of New Brunswick (Bl

This hypothesis was sup- ported by one of the two other published paleomagnetic studies of oolitic hematites: the Silurian Clinton Forma- tion of Alabama had been found to have a higher magnetic susceptibility in the bedding plane than at right angles to it, and its remanence lay close to the bedding plane (Howell et al. 1958, 1960). Oriented samples of Wabana Group and Bell Island Group oolitic hematites were collected and thermally demagnetized prior to testing for anisotropy of acquisi- tion of thermal remanence. However, we could not reproduce the directional results of the earlier study. Instead, the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) initiallv directed toward the north-northeast with a shallo; inclination was found to move syst

In many samples, thermal demagnetization became difficult at tempera- tures above 600°C because the growth of "magnetite" during heating introduced a large spurious component. The upper member of the Peel Sound Formation has been interpreted as deltaic alluvial fan and piedmont deposits with paleocurrent directions towards the west. Miall (1970) distinguished several facies belts, which are, from east to west: (1) conglom- erate facies; (2) conglomerate-sandstone facies: inter- bedded conglomerate, fine to coarse red sandstone and red siltstone, deposited by low sinuosity braided streams; (3) sandstone facies: point bar deposition in high sinuosity streams; (4) sandstone-carbonate facies: red, pink, and buff sandstones, interbedded with dolo- mites deposited in an estuarine environment. Miall (1970) gave a fifth facies, the carbonate facies, but this is now considered to belong to the Drake Bay Formation (Thorsteinsson 1980). Paleomagnetic samples were collected from facies zones 2, 3, and 4. Age The upper member of the Peel Sound Formation is of Early Devonian (late Lochkovian) age (Thorsteinsson 1980). Thermal demagnetization was done stepwise in a large capacity non-inductively wound electric furnace, having a pseudo-zero field of 2 nT (Roy et al. 1969, 1972). The magnetic directions from which the poles are calculated are derived from vector analysis of thermal, chemical, and alternating magnetic field demagnetization results. Normal and reversed polarities are recorded for the northerly pole, whereas the pole at the equator reveals mainly a normal polarity. The position of the pole close to the equator has significant implications for the early Paleozoic apparent polar wander path of the North American craton. It appears that from the Late Cambrian to Early Devonian the craton moved continuously in a counter-clockwise direction that ended abruptly in the Early Devonian when the direction of the motion of the continent was reversed in a very similar manner to what occurred in Late Cambrian times. Although the data for each site are characterized by smearing, individual specimens give very well defined straight-line trajectories that decay to the origin (Fig. 4). Adjacent specimens from the same core most often have similar but not necessarily identical remanence directions (compare 5B 01 and 5A 01, Fig. 4). Two possible mechanisms may have caused the smearing. The individual observed vector may be the resultant of two (or more) actual vectors that have similar remanence characteristics such that any treatment produces straight-line vector trajectories from which the-individual components cannot be separated. On the oher hand, each direction may be a real record of the Earth's field direction, in which case the magnetic component is secondary and was acquired over a MORRIS AND AITKEN 2025 geologically significant period of time. Because the lavas and plug at this locality are extensively altered, without conclusive evidence to the contrary the latter alternative is preferred. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: lower Little Dal Group by Park (1981~). Park reported three directions from sedimentary rocks of the "basinal sequence" of the Little Dal. The magnetite- and hematite-residing LD-A direction is a pre-folding magnetization (pre-Late Cretaceous) which has a mean direction of D = 265", I = -26" (ag5 = 4"). A second magnetization, LD-B, thought to be residing in the red hematite pigment, has a similar mean direction at D = 273", I = -09" (ag5 = 10"). Park (1981~) considered that both these magnetizations were acquired "soon after rock genesis." A third direction, LD-C, (D = 289", I = +79", ag5 = 7"), which characteristically has low blocking temperatures, was suggested to be a "goethite" weathering component of Cretaceous age. The lavas have a much more complicated remanence history. There seems to be little obvious correlation between the remanence directions from the two sections at which the lavas were sampled. At the Keele River area, three well defined groups of remanence directions could be separated. Because of its occurrence in the unaltered lava, and as an univectorial magnetization that resides in both magnetite and hematite, the direction LD-L is considered to provide the best estimate of the magnetic field direction during lava extrusion for the Keele River area. This direction is strongly divergent from the LD-A direction established by Park (198 1 a) for the lower Little Dal Group. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: ere obtained by one of three methods. The reference technique was the least-squares fitting of lines to segments of demagnetization trajectory (Kirschvink 1980). Minimum acceptance criteria adopted for this technique were: a minimum of four points on a line, with a maximum angular deviation of 7.5". Other techniques included least-squares fits to great-circle distributions (Halls 1976), and sequential vector subtractions. For these techniques, which only provided supporting evidence, the minimum acceptance criteria were, respectively: a minimum of four great-circle segments with arc lengths greater than 25", required to define an overprint component; and a maximum angular difference of 10" (determined by vector subtraction) between three sequentially subtracted vectors from the same specimen, the accepted direction being a vector mean of the three components. Site mean directions representative of the individual remanence components present at each site were calculated using the standard Fisher (1953) statistical techniques or the Kirschvink- derived (1980) specimen data directions. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: The Little Dal lavas were sampled at two localities separated by approximately 150 krn. From two sections through the lava sequence near the Keele River area (63"48'N, 231°30'E) 10 sites were obtained for paleomagnetic analysis. Six sites were sampled at a second locality near Coates Lake in the Thundercloud Range (62"24'N, 233"4OtE). At each site at least six 2 in. (5 cm) cores were collected by field drilling. Two specimens were sliced from each core. The bedding orientation at each sampling locality was measured on the nearest sedimentary unit. The difference in structural orientation between the two areas provided a possible fold test of remanence age. At the Keele River sites the beds dip moderately to the west, and at the Coates Lake sites the beds dip steeply to the east. As this folding was probably developed during the Mesozoic orogeny, the fold test does not provide a precise age control of the magnetization; magnetizations passing a positive fold test are merely constrained to the interval Late Precambrian through Cretaceous. The reference technique was the least-squares fitting of lines to segments of demagnetization trajectory (Kirschvink 1980). Minimum acceptance criteria adopted for this technique were: a minimum of four points on a line, with a maximum angular deviation of 7.5". Other techniques included least-squares fits to great-circle distributions (Halls 1976), and sequential vector subtractions. For these techniques, which only provided supporting evidence, the minimum acceptance criteria were, respectively: a minimum of four great-circle segments with arc lengths greater than 25", required to define an overprint component; and a maximum angular difference of 10" (determined by vector subtraction) between three sequentially subtracted vectors from the same specimen, the accepted direction being a vector mean of the three components. Site mean directions representative of the individual remanence components present at each site were calculated using the standard Fisher (1953) statistical techniques or the Kirschvink- derived (1980) specimen data directions. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: The Little Dal lavas were sampled at two localities separated by approximately 150 krn. From two sections through the lava sequence near the Keele River area (63"48'N, 231°30'E) 10 sites were obtained for paleomagnetic analysis. Six sites were sampled at a second locality near Coates Lake in the Thundercloud Range (62"24'N, 233"4OtE). At each site at least six 2 in. (5 cm) cores were collected by field drilling. Two specimens were sliced from each core. The bedding orientation at each sampling locality was measured on the nearest sedimentary unit. The difference in structural orientation between the two areas provided a possible fold test of remanence age. At the Keele River sites the beds dip moderately to the west, and at the Coates Lake sites the beds dip steeply to the east. As this folding was probably developed during the Mesozoic orogeny, the fold test does not provide a precise age control of the magnetization; magnetizations passing a positive fold test are merely constrained to the interval Late Precambrian through Cretaceous. Group 1 units contain a high-coercivity, high-blocking temperature (greater than 520°C) magnetite-dominated remanence characteristic of the complex (D = 280°, 1 = 2", k = 5.5, (rg5 = 11.8", virtual geomagnetic pole = 13"E, 7"s; isolated by both AF and thermal methods), in good agreement with the few previous results bearing on the Late Archean apparent polar wander path for North America. Group 2 units contain a low-coercivity, low-blocking-temperature (less than 310°C) scattered remanence residing in pyrrhotite. Often, both remanences coexist in a single lithology at a given site. Group 3 units contain distributed coercivity and blocking-temperature remanences, again residing in magnetite, that are more scattered but statistically identical to the mean group 1 direction. The order of magnetic blocking appears to have been group 1 before group 3 before group 2. The geologic setting of the Ghost Range suggests that it has remained essentially stable since emplacement and therefore the group 1 direction appears to reliably represent a Late Archean paleomagnetic pole. Introduction I Several Late Proterozoic apparent polar wander , (APW) trends for the North American craton have I become well established in recent years. Particularly ; well known are the Logan Loop (Robertson and Fahrig 8 1971) and the Grenville Loop (McWilliams and Dunlop 1975). The Logan Loop is a broad APW loop that has 1 been defined from numerous studies in the Lake Superior region, the Grand Canyon (Elston and Gromme 1974), and other areas of the craton. Asymmetric reversals have been observed in the lower and middle Keweenawan age rocks that define the I northern apex of the Logan Loop. Much careful work 1 has been done in order to explain the origin of these 1 asymmetric reversals (e.g., Palmer et al. 1981; Halls and Palmer 1981; Pesonen and Nevanlinna 1981) and 1 they may be due to non-dipole behavior of the Earth's magnetic field during this interval. Based on such a non-dipol

ed a modified Logan Loop that is greatly reduced in 1 size from that originally proposed. The descending limb of the Logan Loop is defined by poles from middle and 1 upper Keweenawan volcanics and sediments. A critical link between the Keweenawan poles and the later Grenville poles is provided by secondary poles from the Middle River section (Orienta Formation) and the Fond du Lac Sandstone (Watts 1981). The Grenville poles, once considered as evidence for convergence between the Grenville Province and the North American craton, have been shown to represent magnetizations reset during the cooling of the Grenville Province (McWilliams and Dunlop 1975). Thus they postdate the orogenic event and must be considered cratonic North American poles. In addition to the well established Keweenawan and Grenville APW path segments, some poorly dated magnetizations, many demonstrably secondary, have been used to define an APW path termed the "Hadrynian track" (Morris and Roy 1977). The Hadrynian track involves major APW that begins with the 950Ma Grenville poles, moves over the present north pole, and terminates about 180" away from the Grenville poles in the equatorial Atlantic Ocean with poles dated at 670Ma. The Bayfield Group overlies the Oronto Group; together these two groups comprise upper Keweenawan sediments, which overlie Middle Keweenawan vol- canic~ that are generally thought to have been extruded at about 1100Ma (Irving and McGlynn 1976). The age of the Bayfield Group and its probable equivalent in Michigan, the Jacobsville Sandstone, is constrained to be younger than middle Keweenawan and older than overlying Upper Cambrian sediments. Paleomagnetic results from the Jacobsville (Roy and Robertson 1978) show that the Jacobsville pole falls on the APW path in agreement with a late Keweenawan age. The maior structure in the area is the Keweenaw trough, wiich appears to underlie most of Lake Superior (Halls and West 1971). This trough continues to the southwest under Paleozoic cover and is aligned with the mid-continent gravity high. The Keweenaw trough is considered to represent a failed intracontinental rift (Chase and Gilmer 1973). The Bayfield sandstones are bounded to the south by the Douglas Fault, a high-angle reverse fault that puts these sandstones in fault contact with middle Keweenawan volcanics. plications for red bed diagenesis and Late Precambrian apparent polar wander of North America CHAD MCCABE AND ROB VAN BR VOO Department of Geological Sciences, The University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109, U.S.A. Received May 4, 1982 Revision accepted August 18, 1982 Two components of magnetization have been isolated from Chequamegon Sandstone samples using chemical demagnetization. A characteristic magnetization resides in magnetite of detrital origin. The pole calculated from this magnetization is 12.3"S, 177.7"E (K = 111.5, Ag5 = 4.6'). This pole lies with other poles of late Keweenawan age and is very close to the Jacobsville Sandstone poles. A secondary magnetization resides in authigenic hematite and yields a pole close to the present north pole. This high-latitude pole is known from an earlier study of the Chequamegon and has been used as evidence for the Hadrynian APW track. However, most if not all of the high-latitude poles that define the Hadrynian track are secondary and undated. Our preferred alternative to the Hadrynian track is that the high-latitude poles are recent remagnetizations and that the antipodal equatorial poles that mark its end points represent field reversals. Based on such a non-dipole model, Pesonen and Nevanlinna have offered a modified Logan Loop that is greatly reduced in 1 size from that originally proposed. The descending limb of the Logan Loop is defined by poles from middle and 1 upper Keweenawan volcanics and sediments. A critical link between the Keweenawan poles and the later Grenville poles is provided by secondary poles from the Middle River section (Orienta Formation) and the Fond du Lac Sandstone (Watts 1981). The Grenville poles, once considered as evidence for convergence between the Grenville Province and the North American craton, have been shown to represent magnetizations reset during the cooling of the Grenville Province (McWilliams and Dunlop 1975). Thus they postdate the orogenic event and must be considered cratonic North American poles. In addition to the well established Keweenawan and Grenville APW path segments, some poorly dated magnetizations, many demonstrably secondary, have been used to define an APW path termed the "Hadrynian track" (Morris and Roy 1977). The Hadrynian t

tinent with respect to the pole would be about 30 cm/year, an extremely high rate compared with those known for the Phanerozoic. Since the high-latitude poles that define these APW paths are undated, doubt must remain concerning their validity. Nevertheless, Piper (1981) used his North American APW path to propose a particular reconstruc- tion of a Late Precambrian supercontinent. The importance of such reconstructions in global tectonic studies warrants the close examination of the poles that at present define these APW paths. One critical high-latitude pole in both Hadrynian track models is the one derived from the Chequamegon Sandstone (DuBois 1962). This pole was calculated from a small number of samples that were subjected to minimal thermal cleaning. The present study was undertaken to apply modem paleomagnetic methods to test whether this earlier Chequamegon pole is the result of a primary or a secondary magnetization. Geologic setting The Chequamegon Sandstone is the uppermost unit of the Bayfield Group. It lies near the axis of the Keweenaw trough in horizontal beds that crop out on the Bayfield Peninsula and adjacent Apostle Islands in Wisconsin (Fig. 1). During the past few years, interpretations of the geology of the island has undergone rapid changes based on Wilson's (1966) hypothesis of a proto-Atlantic Ocean and the current ideas on plate tectonics. The revised interpretations are efficiently reviewed in a series of articles by Williams et al. (1972, 1974). They fitted the geology of the island into various tectono-stratigraphic zones, each zone having a characteristic tectonic, stratigraphic, and metamorphic signature. These zones, labelled A-H from west to east (Fig. I), are extrapolated (Williams 1978) to cover the full Appalachians to their southern extremity in the United States. Of the various tectono-stratigraphic zones, the Gander Zone is quite complex geologically and is characterized by highly metamorphosed and poly- deformed rocks. During the past few years, interpretations of the geology of the island has undergone rapid changes based on Wilson's (1966) hypothesis of a proto-Atlantic Ocean and the current ideas on plate tectonics. The revised interpretations are efficiently reviewed in a series of articles by Williams et al. (1972, 1974). They fitted the geology of the island into various tectono-stratigraphic zones, each zone having a characteristic tectonic, stratigraphic, and metamorphic signature. These zones, labelled A-H from west to east (Fig. I), are extrapolated (Williams 1978) to cover the full Appalachians to their southern extremity in the United States. Earth Sci., 20, 246-258 (1983) [Traduit par le journal] Introduction The tectonic history of the Grenville Province has been interpreted, on the basis of paleomagnetic evi- dence, by several authors (e.g . , Fahrig et al. 1974; Irving et al. 1974; McWilliams and Dunlop 1978; Dunlop et al. 1980). With few exceptions, however, paleomagnetic sampling has been confined to the western portion of the Grenville Province in Ontario and the Grenville Front region in eastern Quebec and Labrador. Hence, it is difficult to obtain a coherent picture of the paleomagnetism of the province as a . whole. In this study, alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization results are reported for the Lac St-Jean anorthosite and surrounding monzonites, granites, and diabase dikes from the central portion of the Grenville Province. Geology The Lac St-Jean anorthosite forms part of a chain of similar in

orthosite intrusion. The Ste. Marguerite monzonite (Fig. 1) is an apple green, fine- to medium-grained rock containing uralitized pyroxene. Rb/Sr work suggests, from initial "~r/~~Sr ratios, that this rock was re-equilibrated about 1100 Ma ago (Frith and Doig 1973). Granodiorite in the Anse St. Jean area (site 29) is similar and has been grouped with the Ste. Marguerite monzonite. The quartz diorite gneiss in the same vicinity (site 28) probably hosts the monzonite-granodiorite rocks. The Chamouchouane monzonite (Fig. 1) is a fairly massive subcircular body surrounded by charnockitic gneiss (Benoit 1960). The monzonite is intrusive, and a Rb/Sr isochron dates its consolidation at 148 1 ? 94 Ma (Frith and Doig 1973). ogical Survey of Canada, Ottawa, ~kt., Canada KIA OE8 Received May 14, 1982 Revision accepted October 19, 1982 Northern Baffin Island is intersected by spectacular swarms of predominantly northwesterly trending diabase dykes. Cross-cutting relationships, K-Ar ages, and paleomagnetic contact tests indicate that these dykes represent at least two major episodes of Hadrynian igneous activity. The Borden dykes were emplaced during the earlier of these episodes. They are about 950 Ma oId and have a paleomagnetic pole position of 153.3"E, 26.7"S, Sm = 8.6", Sp = 6.1". The later episode saw the emplacement of the previous! y defined Franklin dykes, which are about 750 Ma old. The newly defined Borden pole lies at the southern extremity of the Grenville Loop and has an age consistent with poles of similar position that were derived from rocks of the Orcnville Province. All of the dykes probably reflect tension acting in an east-northeast-west-southwest direction. The directions of thick northwest trending dykes, which form a considerable angle to that expected from east-northeast tension, are thought to have been controlled by earlier (circa 1200 Ma) fractures of the Borden fault zones. The two main surges of magma may coincide with two periods of Hadrynian uplift in the Boothia

Other dyke sites A number of sites cannot be classified paleomagneti- cally as either Franklin or Borden. Group 1-the Tremblay Sound dyke This group consists of sites 45 and 7901,7902,7903 (Fig. 1; Table 1). These have well grouped, stable, northwest down directions (Fig. 9) and may represent a single, en Cchelon dyke with a trend usual for the Borden dykes. There are a number of possible explanations for the magnetization direction. The pole position is north of the Franklin pole for Borden Peninsula. It could therefore reflect post-Franklin remagnetization during a later thermal event. This is unlikely because there is no evidence of such an event in neighbouring dykes or sediments, nor is there evidence of two components in any of the samples, except for a viscous component probably related to the recent Earth's field. The area is now flooded so that future work is not possible. The limited geological and statistical data base makes interpretation of the results necessarily tentative. The dikes yield an A component pole at 84W, 74% from magnetization residing in higher stability domains, which likely reflects emplacement either at -2150 or -1825 or - 1650 Ma ago, and a B component pole at 33W, 4"s residing in lower stability domains, which likely reflects metamorphism during the Hudsonian Orogeny at - 1725 Ma, or, less likely, during Grenvillian uplift at -975 Ma. - 1725 Ma. This fits with the high blocking temperatures of up to 550°C for the component. Con- versely, the B antipole also lies near the Grenville Orogeny loop of the APW path at -975 Ma and could be an uplift component. This fits with the subgreenschist alteration at most of the dikes and Park's (1977) observation of similar Grenvillian uplift components in most rock units of the Labrador Trough. Volcanics The C and D components of the Archean volcanics are both thermally unblocked at -555 + 15°C. Although the C component is more prevalent than the D, both appear equally stable, and hence either may be older. Also, their high blocking temperatures suggest that both were set before or during the Kenoran Orogeny, which deformed and regionally metamorphosed the volcanics prior to -2450 Ma. The volcanics strike at 260 + 10" and dip at 62 + 8"s at all sampling sites, so that the fold test is equivocal. Microfold structures show that the volcanics plunge at 35 + 5W. The area is now flooded so that future work is not possible. The limited geological and statistical data base makes interpretation of the results necessarily tentative. The dikes yield an A component pole at 84W, 74% from magnetization residing in higher stability domains, which likely reflects emplacement either at -2150 or -1825 or - 1650 Ma ago, and a B component pole at 33W, 4"s residing in lower stability domains, which likely reflects metamorphism during the Hudsonian Orogeny at - 1725 Ma, or, less likely, during Grenvillian uplift at -975 Ma. The volcanics appear to yield a prefolding C component pole at 28"W, 49"s that dates ex

- 1725 Ma. This fits with the high blocking temperatures of up to 550°C for the component. Con- versely, the B antipole also lies near the Grenville Orogeny loop of the APW path at -975 Ma and could be an uplift component. This fits with the subgreenschist alteration at most of the dikes and Park's (1977) observation of similar Grenvillian uplift components in most rock units of the Labrador Trough. Volcanics The C and D components of the Archean volcanics are both thermally unblocked at -555 + 15°C. Although the C component is more prevalent than the D, both appear equally stable, and hence either may be older. Also, their high blocking temperatures suggest that both were set before or during the Kenoran Orogeny, which deformed and regionally metamorphosed the volcanics prior to -2450 Ma. The volcanics strike at 260 + 10" and dip at 62 + 8"s at all sampling sites, so that the fold test is equivocal. Microfold structures show that the volcanics plunge at 35 + 5W. - 1725 Ma. This fits with the high blocking temperatures of up to 550°C for the component. Con- versely, the B antipole also lies near the Grenville Orogeny loop of the APW path at -975 Ma and could be an uplift component. This fits with the subgreenschist alteration at most of the dikes and Park's (1977) observation of similar Grenvillian uplift components in most rock units of the Labrador Trough. Volcanics The C and D components of the Archean volcanics are both thermally unblocked at -555 + 15°C. Although the C component is more prevalent than the D, both appear equally stable, and hence either may be older. Also, their high blocking temperatures suggest that both were set before or during the Kenoran Orogeny, which deformed and regionally metamorphosed the volcanics prior to -2450 Ma. The volcanics strike at 260 + 10" and dip at 62 + 8"s at all sampling sites, so that the fold test is equivocal. Microfold structures show that the volcanics plunge at 35 + 5W. Con- versely, the B antipole also lies near the Grenville Orogeny loop of the APW path at -975 Ma and could be an uplift component. This fits with the subgreenschist alteration at most of the dikes and Park's (1977) observation of similar Grenvillian uplift components in most rock units of the Labrador Trough. The tilt-corrected mean direction for this data set is D = 331°, I = +47" (N = 20 specimens, ag5 = 4"). This corresponds to a paleomagnetic pole position at 113"E, 59"N. Of especial importance is the necessity of establishing the age of the MN-B pole: if the MN-B pole dates from the time of sedimentation then this implies that at least some of the common belt poles are not original but reset secondary magnetizations. er Belt-Purcell formations in the Glacier National Park - Clark Range area. However, the distribution of these oxida- tion classes within individual flows is not this broad. Flows whose initial remanence is either clearly normal or reverse contain oxides at the high end of the oxidation spectrum (types 2 and 3), whereas flows whose initial remanence is steep-down and that remains so upon either AF or thermal demagnetization are dominated by magnetites lacking or poor in exsolved ilmenite or its decomposition products. Flows possessing the steep- down characteristic remanence thermally unblock at temperatures below 570°C and lack hematite. The time of acquisition of the steep-down component is problematical. Because most of the sites possessing the steep-down component as the characteristic rema- nence occur at or near reversal boundaries it could be argued that these remanences were formed by partial baking of normal flows by reverse flows and vice versa. In most previous paleomagnetic studies of Franklin rocks (Robertson and Baragar 1972; Fahrig and Schwarz 1973; Palmer and Hayatsu 1975; Park 1981) a steep- down component of remanence is observed but in most cases this component could be removed by modest AF demagnetization. This component of remanence was ascribed to viscous acquisition in the present or Bruhnes field. However, in some of the Franklin rocks of the present study, the steep-down component completely dominates the entire coercivity and blocking tempera- ture spectra. It is hard to envisage a mechanism whereby viscous remanence, carried by magnetite and not hema- tite, acquired at ambient temperatures (and for these rocks much of the annual cycle is at subzero tem- peratures) could completely replace an older thermal or thermo-chemical remanent magnetization. Furthermore the derived paleopoles from eastern Arctic sites show a small but significant difference from those derived from western Arctic sites (Palmer and Hayatsu 1975). Recent paleomagnetic work on Franklin diabases from the Brock Inlier of the western Arctic (Park 1981) has reconfirmed this regional difference. Palmer and Hayatsu (1975) suggested that this difference in pole position reflected a real age difference in the time of igneous activity in the western and eastern Arctic. This proposition presupposed that primary remanences un- contaminated by any secondary overprint were obtained in the early studies of the western Arctic samples. Because both polarities have now been obtained from the Natkusiak basalts but, unlike the eastern Arctic dikes, the polarities are not consistently antiparallel, it seems equally plausible that the difference in pole positions is related to a bias in the final directions caused by the steep-down overprint. In most previous paleomagnetic studies of Franklin rocks (Robertson and Baragar 1972; Fahrig and Schwarz 1973; Palmer and Hayatsu 1975; Park 1981) a steep- down component of remanence is observed but in most cases this component could be removed by modest AF demagnetization. This component of remanence was ascribed to viscous acquisition in the present or Bruhnes field. However, in some of the Franklin rocks of the present study, the steep-down component completely dominates the entire coercivity and blocking tempera- ture spectra. In a preserved thickness of about 740 m of Natkusiak flows the polarity changes upward in roughly successive thirds of the section from east and slightly downward (reverse), to west and slightly downward (normal), to east and slightly upward (reverse). Thus there is a double reversal in the section but the lower reverse direction is badly contaminated by a downward directed overprint. At three sites this steep downward component persists after cleaning. Dolerite polarities, except for one that is normal, cluster in the east-down (reverse) direction close to the lower reverse direction of the lavas and steeply downward, similar to the overprint direction in the flows. The downward component can be correlated with evidence of low initial oxidation and more severe alteration in the corresponding samples and may be related to burial metamorphism. The reverse direction of the upper lavas, being from the freshest parts of the section and closest in direction to the exact reversals recorded in Franklin dikes from Baffin Island, is believed to be most reliable. Furthermore, this mechanism could not be applied to the dolerite sills that are separated by thick successions of intervening sedimentary strata. In most previous paleomagnetic studies of Franklin rocks (Robertson and Baragar 1972; Fahrig and Schwarz 1973; Palmer and Hayatsu 1975; Park 1981) a steep- down component of remanence is observed but in most cases this component could be removed by modest AF demagnetization. This component of remanence was ascribed to viscous acquisition in the present or Bruhnes field. However, in some of the Franklin rocks of the present study, the steep-down component completely dominates the entire coercivity and blocking tempera- ture spectra. It is hard to envisage a mechanism whereby viscous remanence, carried by magnetite and not hema- tite, acquired at ambient temperatures (and for these rocks much of the annual cycle is at subzero tem- peratures) could completely replace an older thermal or thermo-chemical remanent magnetization.
